summary: I read all 16 in-scope files and traced the submission, feed, confirmation, dashboard, and complaint paths. P1 findings exist: registry data can route PII to untrusted or non-opt-out pages, generic submissions can be reported as successful without an opt-out, and complaint files expose PII to other local accounts under a typical umask.

findings.title: Complaint files inherit permissive default permissions
findings.what: The complaint directory and TXT files are created without owner-only modes; the PDF writer also receives no restricted mode. With a typical 022 umask, files are readable by other local accounts.
findings.trigger: Run complaint generation on Linux or macOS with overdue entries and the default umask.
findings.impact: Other local users can read the complainant’s name, location, email, and phone from the generated reports.
findings.fix: Create the directory with mode 0700 and restrict both TXT and PDF files to 0600.

findings.title: Registry URLs can direct the browser to arbitrary hosts
findings.what: Feed URLs are accepted if they merely start with `http`; they are later navigated to and their forms may be filled with the user's PII. Neither private addresses nor redirects are restricted.
findings.trigger: A registry row contains an attacker-controlled, loopback, private, or link-local URL, or redirects to one.
findings.impact: The browser can reach internal services or send PII to a malicious form during the unattended run.
findings.fix: Validate the broker target before navigation, reject non-public addresses, and revalidate every redirect against an approved broker origin.

findings.title: Registry homepage URLs are processed as opt-out forms
findings.what: The feed’s `method` is ignored when rows are added. A homepage classified as `manual` is still sent to the generic form filler, which can fill and submit a newsletter or marketing form.
findings.trigger: A registry lists a broker’s homepage rather than a dedicated opt-out page, and that page has a generic form.
findings.impact: The tool sends the user's name and contact details to an unintended form instead of requesting removal.
findings.fix: Only enqueue verified opt-out URLs classified as `direct-form`; keep manual or homepage entries out of automatic submission.

findings.title: A successful button click is treated as an accepted opt-out
findings.what: After `submitForm()` returns true, the runner reports success unless it detects an email-confirmation message. It does not require positive success evidence or reject ordinary validation/server errors; a click can return true even when browser validation prevents submission.
findings.trigger: A generic form has an unfilled required field or returns an error without email-confirmation wording.
findings.impact: The tool records `lastSuccess` and suppresses retries while reporting the broker as opted out, although no removal request was accepted.
findings.fix: Require explicit post-submit success evidence; report failures or unknown outcomes as errors or unverified.

findings.title: SMTP acceptance is recorded as removal success
findings.what: A successful `sendMail()` call proves the message was accepted by the mail transport, not that the broker removed the data. The code records it as `lastSuccess`, which starts the 90-day skip window.
findings.trigger: SMTP accepts an opt-out email but the broker ignores it or does not complete the request.
findings.impact: The dashboard can count the broker as opted out and the tool delays follow-up for 90 days without evidence of removal.
findings.fix: Track email delivery separately from confirmed removal and avoid counting delivery as an opt-out success.

findings.title: Preview output includes raw form values
findings.what: Preview mode formats every populated input value into `detail` and sends it to `logResult()`, which prints it to stdout; the dashboard also streams child output.
findings.trigger: Run `--preview` from the CLI or dashboard on a form containing the user's details.
findings.impact: PII appears in terminal output, dashboard streams, and any service or container log collector capturing stdout.
findings.fix: Show field names and fill status only; redact all field values in preview output.

findings.title: Freeze updates can overwrite concurrent opt-out state
findings.what: The freeze handler reads and rewrites the entire state file without the runner’s process lock. Atomic rename prevents torn files but does not prevent a stale read-modify-write from winning.
findings.trigger: Toggle a freeze target while a watcher run is updating `state.json`.
findings.impact: The dashboard write can erase newer opt-out history, leading to repeated submissions or lost pending state.
findings.fix: Use the same state lock and shared save path, or store freeze status separately from opt-out state.

findings.title: A data-access request can trigger a deletion complaint
findings.what: `resolveRequestedAt()` prioritizes `knowRequestedAt`, even though that timestamp records a disclosure request, not an erasure request. Complaint generation then describes it as a verified deletion request.
findings.trigger: A broker has an overdue right-to-know request but no deletion request recorded.
findings.impact: The tool can generate a regulator complaint containing the user's PII and a false claim that the broker ignored a deletion request.
findings.fix: Do not use `knowRequestedAt` for deletion complaints; handle overdue access requests with a separate, accurate complaint type.

findings.title: Confirmation navigation trusts redirects after validating the initial URL
findings.what: The extracted URL is checked against the broker host, but `page.goto()` follows redirects without checking the final destination; the code later records success after any non-throwing navigation.
findings.trigger: A broker-hosted confirmation link or open redirect sends the browser to an unrelated or private address.
findings.impact: The confirmation workflow can visit an unintended destination and mark the broker successful without evidence that removal was confirmed.
findings.fix: Restrict redirect targets and final URLs to approved broker hosts, and require explicit confirmation evidence before recording success.

findings.title: Multi-person complaint files overwrite each other
findings.what: Complaint filenames include only broker and agency, so complaints for different people sharing the same broker and agency resolve to the same paths.
findings.trigger: Two configured people have overdue entries for the same broker and regime.
findings.impact: The later TXT/PDF overwrites the earlier person’s report, leaving one complaint missing.
findings.fix: Include a sanitized person identifier or unique suffix in each complaint filename.
